TPF induction: docetaxel, cisplatin and fluorouracilNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00315

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.

Record the actual date, treatment phase, medicines given, any delay or dose change, blood tests and next appointments. The treating service confirms all entries; this does not replace its clinical record.

changes.text: Regimen-specific side effectsYour anatomical side-effect mapA picture of side effectsMatch each symptom box to its numbered body location. Tell your team about new symptoms.1Hair and scalpDocetaxelHair thinning or loss can occur. Ask about scalp care and practical support.3Mouth and throatDocetaxel + 5-FUSoreness or ulcers (mucositis) can make eating and drinking difficult. Contact the team for pain or poor intake.5Blood and infectionDocetaxel + cisplatin + 5-FULow white cells can cause serious infection; low platelets cause bruising or bleeding; anaemia causes fatigue. Call for fever or sudden illness.7Stomach and bowelAll three chemotherapy drugsNausea and vomiting can occur; 5-FU may cause severe diarrhoea. Persistent symptoms can cause dehydration and need prompt help.9Hands, feet and nervesDocetaxel + cisplatinNumbness or tingling (peripheral neuropathy) can persist. Report difficulty with buttons, walking or balance before another dose.1234567892Ears and hearingCisplatinRinging or hearing loss can persist (ototoxicity). Report a change before the next dose.4Heart and chest5-FUChest pain can signal a heart effect (cardiotoxicity). Seek urgent assessment during or after the infusion.6Kidneys and fluidsCisplatinKidney injury and mineral changes can occur. Prescribed fluids and blood tests help protect you; report reduced urine or inability to drink.8Skin, nails, hands and feetDocetaxel + 5-FUDocetaxel may affect nails and retain fluid; 5-FU may cause painful palms or soles (hand–foot syndrome). Report swelling, pain or skin breakdown.Selected effects, not every possible effect or a prediction. Blood-count, skin and line markers are schematic. Number and text carry meaning; colour is decorative.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, sudden confusion, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms needs urgent assessment even if dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (a medicine-processing enzyme) (DPD) testing was normal. Report reduced urine, hearing change, ringing in the ears or new numbness promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112 or 999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.

This chemotherapy is given before definitive treatment to shrink or control the head and neck cancer. The team explains how induction fits your overall treatment aim and why this particular schedule is appropriate.

Docetaxel stabilises tiny structures called microtubules. Cells need these to separate their chromosomes during division; disrupting the process can stop cancer cells multiplying. Healthy dividing cells are also affected.
What to watch forTake prescribed steroid premedication. Report fever, lasting numbness, swelling, sore nails or infusion symptoms.

Cisplatin links strands of DNA, the instructions inside cells, making it harder for cancer cells to repair damage and divide. Healthy cells may also be affected. Kidney function, hearing, blood counts and nerve symptoms help the team decide whether the next dose is safe.
What to watch forReport reduced urine, persistent vomiting, tinnitus, hearing change or new tingling.

Fluorouracil, often shortened to 5-FU, interferes with the building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, which cells need to grow. It runs through a vein over the prescribed hours. Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) is an enzyme that breaks it down. Testing for DPD deficiency before treatment reduces risk but cannot rule out every severe reaction.
What to watch forReport severe diarrhoea, mouth sores, chest pain, sudden confusion, sore palms or soles, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms.

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. Use your treating service’s written temperature threshold and urgent-contact plan. Fever, shivering or sudden illness can be serious even without a high temperature. Do not wait for the next visit. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure needs emergency help: call 112 or 999.

Docetaxel and cisplatin are given in the unit with prescribed premedication, fluids and anti-sickness medicines. Fluorouracil begins. Confirm whether your prescription uses one continuous 96-hour fluorouracil infusion or four daily 22-hour infusions; the unit writes down connection, change and disconnection times. Tell the team if steroid doses were missed, you feel unwell or you have new symptoms before treatment starts.

Fluorouracil 1,000 mg/m² per day runs continuously over 96 hours on Days 1–4; the source also allows a separate 22-hour infusion on each of those four days. Only trained staff connect, program, change or disconnect the infusion. Follow the line and pump instructions. Call for leakage, pain, swelling, damage or an infusion that appears to finish unexpectedly or stop.

Follow the prescribed home medicine and growth-factor plan. Side effects may continue or appear between visits; no day is guaranteed free of risk. Keep blood-test and review appointments and call promptly if unwell.
From preparing the line to coming home after disconnection. Your team arranges the appointments and shows you what to do.
Your team chooses the venous access device and teaches its care, including a port or peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) if used.
Confirm whether your prescription uses one continuous 96-hour fluorouracil infusion or four daily 22-hour infusions; the unit writes down connection, change and disconnection times.
Only trained staff connect, program or change the infusion. Do not calculate or alter the rate.
Call for leakage, pain, swelling, damage, disconnection, unexpected completion or a pump that appears not to run. Follow the unit’s device-specific emergency instructions.
The actual connection time and selected infusion duration determine completion. Do not disconnect or reconnect the line yourself.
Keep dressing, flushing and review appointments; report redness, pain, fever or swelling.

A port is a small chamber beneath the skin, usually on the chest, attached to a tube ending in a large vein. A special needle goes through the skin into the port when it is used. A PICC enters a vein in the upper arm; a short section remains outside under a dressing. Both can deliver a home infusion. Your team helps choose the device and teaches its care.

Tell the team about allergies, blood thinners, infections and any other cancer medicines. Follow the instructions about eating, drinking and transport; do not stop medicines yourself. Port placement uses local anaesthetic, sometimes with sedation or general anaesthetic. The team explains the procedure and risks, including infection, bleeding, clots and insertion complications. Ask how to manage discomfort, protect the wound and resume activity. Report increasing pain, redness, swelling, discharge or fever.

The nurse checks the line and treatment, secures the connection and dressing, and starts the pump. Before leaving, you should have the disconnection location and time, contact numbers including out of hours, and the written spill instructions. Ask to be shown what normal pump progress looks like. You do not need to calculate a rate.

Use the supplied carrier and the position recommended for your pump. Keep tubing free from pulling and kinks. Ask how to place the pump safely for sleep and how to protect the line and dressing when washing. Do not immerse it or swim. Avoid direct heat and cold. An elastomeric pump has a balloon that shrinks slowly and may have no alarm; an electronic pump has different instructions. Follow the instructions for the device you actually receive.

Keep the appointment even if the pump looks empty, unless the team changes the plan. Staff check the pump and line and arrange safe disposal. After flushing and other line care as required, the port needle may be removed and a small dressing applied. The implanted port stays in place until a separate removal procedure is arranged. A PICC remains in place and needs scheduled dressing and flushing care.

Call the team immediately if the pump leaks, is damaged, finishes unexpectedly early, appears not to run, or the line disconnects. Follow the emergency or spill steps you have been specifically taught, including use of a clamp if instructed. Do not reconnect, change settings or disconnect the pump yourself. Keep other people away from leaked medicine. If medicine touches skin, rinse it off and wash with soap and water, then seek advice.

Contact oncology immediately for pain or swelling around the line, a wet/loose dressing, redness, fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell. A painful swollen arm or neck needs urgent advice. Severe chest pain, major breathing difficulty or collapse: call 112 / 999. Do not wait for pump disconnection or the next clinic visit.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.
Confirm the exact regimen, treatment aim, baseline tests, transport, support medicines and verified urgent contact numbers. Bring a full medicine list and any hearing, nerve or swallowing concerns.
Keep one calendar for blood tests, treatment and any radiation, dental, nutrition or swallowing appointments. If an appointment is cancelled, ask the relevant teams to agree the revised plan.
Tell the team about travel, cost, work, caring responsibilities, communication or reading needs. Ask whether a support person or interpreter can attend and how treatment changes will be explained.
Check the next blood-test and treatment dates, medicine instructions and whom to call if unwell. Have the service confirm the daytime, out-of-hours and backup contact routes.

The source premedication is dexamethasone 8 mg by mouth twice daily for three days, starting the day before docetaxel, with at least three doses taken before infusion. It helps reduce allergy and fluid retention. Follow your prescribed plan. If doses are missed or you cannot swallow them, contact the unit before attending; the clinician decides the alternative.

Cisplatin has a high risk of nausea and vomiting. The team provides preventive and rescue anti-sickness treatment. Have all steroid doses reconciled on one list so the docetaxel premedication and anti-sickness prescription do not lead to accidental duplication.

Growth-factor support (G-CSF) is required with every cycle of this regimen. Your team prescribes the product, dose and injection dates. Confirm who gives it and whom to contact if a dose is missed; it reduces risk but does not remove the need to call for fever or sudden illness.

Cisplatin requires prescribed fluids before and after treatment. Oral hydration is encouraged for the following 24 hours, adapted to your heart, kidney and swallowing needs. Ask for a practical individual fluid plan and call for much less urine, persistent vomiting or inability to drink.

An antibiotic may be added by the treating team according to the regimen and your situation. It is not a medicine to start from an old supply. Confirm the name, start and stop dates and important interactions; infection symptoms still need urgent contact.

Use the mouth-care and pain plan. Report ulcers, infection, poor intake or weight loss early. Dietitian and speech and language support can tailor intake and swallowing advice; arrange dental assessment before planned head and neck radiation.

Discuss fertility, pregnancy, breastfeeding and the medicine-specific duration of contraception before treatment. Bring medicines, supplements and allergies and check before adding over-the-counter or herbal products.
Keep your diagnosis, treatment name and agreed goal with your records.
Ask where the cancer started, what the biopsy shows and how far it has spread. Site, stage, previous treatment and general health affect the available options.
Induction treatment for stage III or IV non-metastatic squamous cell cancer of the head and neck, within a planned course of definitive treatment.

Your team explains any HPV/p16, Epstein–Barr virus or other tumour tests appropriate to your cancer site. Not every site needs the same tests. These are different from blood, kidney and other medicine safety checks.
Discuss the whole plan and each stage before consenting.

This chemotherapy is given before definitive treatment to shrink or control the head and neck cancer. The team explains how induction fits your overall treatment aim and why this particular schedule is appropriate. Ask how the expected benefit and burdens compare with suitable alternatives and with your priorities.

The clinician may delay, change or stop treatment because of symptoms, test results, response or your preferences. Record which component is affected and what must happen before restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription.
Plan the appointments and practical support around the exact prescription.

Docetaxel 75 mg/m² and cisplatin 75 mg/m² are given on Day 1. Fluorouracil 1,000 mg/m² per day runs continuously over 96 hours on Days 1–4; the source also allows a separate 22-hour infusion on each of those four days. Induction repeats every 21 days for 3 planned cycles unless cancer progression or unacceptable side effects require a change. This 21-day picture describes induction only. Steroid premedication starts the day before docetaxel. Infusion finish times depend on the chosen prescription and actual start time; later radiation or chemoradiation has a separate calendar.

Write the actual date, phase, medicines and any change. Record a delayed or omitted dose clearly; it is not automatically made up. The wallet card gives a brief record and the passport keeps the fuller history.
Use the written home plan and contact route.
Effects may begin during treatment or develop later, and some build up over repeated doses. Call for a new, severe or worsening symptom even when a calendar calls the day a recovery day.

Keep prevention medicines, rescue medicines and regular medicines together on one reconciled written list. Record what you take and whether it helps. Do not double a missed dose or reuse an old prescription unless your treating team instructs you.

Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, sudden confusion, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms needs urgent assessment even if DPD testing was normal. Report reduced urine, hearing change, ringing in the ears or new numbness promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112 or 999.
Dental preparation and gentle daily care reduce avoidable problems.

Arrange dental assessment before head and neck radiation. The dental and oncology teams decide what treatment is needed and how much healing time is required; do not schedule extractions independently.

Follow the prescribed brushing, fluoride, rinse and pain-relief advice. Report ulcers, infection, new bleeding, difficulty wearing dentures or worsening jaw opening. Avoid starting a new mouthwash without checking if the mouth is sore.

Dry mouth can increase dental problems and some radiation effects last. Keep regular dental care and tell any future dentist that you have had head and neck radiation before invasive treatment. Your radiation/dental team plans any procedure.
The aim is adequate intake and comfort during treatment.
Record weight and report food or drink becoming harder to manage. Pain, taste change, dry mouth or nausea can each need a different response; a dietitian can adapt the plan to you.

The team may suggest food fortification, supplements or tube feeding when intake or swallowing safety requires it. A tube is a support option, not a judgement about how well you have tried to eat. Training and follow-up are needed.
Ask for a realistic drinking plan that accounts for kidney/heart problems and any feeding tube. Persistent vomiting, dizziness, markedly reduced urine or inability to drink needs urgent contact.
A speech and language therapist can help protect function.
Report coughing or choking with food or drink, a wet-sounding voice after swallowing, food sticking or repeated chest infections. The team may need to assess aspiration risk and safe textures.
Do swallowing or jaw exercises only as taught for your situation. Treatment and recovery can change what is comfortable and safe. Ask for reassessment when symptoms change.
Tell the team about changes in speech, voice or hearing. Ask for written instructions, communication aids, an interpreter or help involving a support person.
Practical adjustments can make the plan easier to follow.
Balance rest with manageable activity according to your ability and team advice. Ask for help if weakness, falls, sleep difficulty or pain interferes with daily life.
Ask for support to stop smoking and discuss alcohol with the team. Mouth irritation, medicine interactions and head and neck recovery can change what is safe for you.

Tell the team about anxiety, appearance or intimacy concerns, finances, travel and caring responsibilities. Ask which local supports are available; resources can be added to your record when confirmed.
The last treatment and the end of recovery are different milestones.

Your team sets the examination and imaging plan for your cancer and symptoms. Record who arranges each test and who will explain the result. New or worsening symptoms should be reported rather than saved for the next routine scan.

Keep the regimen name, treatment dates, ongoing medicines and relevant alert information. Tell future clinicians and dentists about head and neck radiation if you receive it, and about any persistent kidney, hearing, nerve or swallowing problem.
Keep essential instructions available on paper.

The three-page companion gives the essentials. Use the passport for the agreed plan, visits, test results, symptoms and questions. The wallet QR opens this exact treatment’s further information; it contains no personal clinical record.

Have the treating service enter and verify daytime, out-of-hours and backup numbers before relying on this pack. Keep the written contact and temperature instructions where you and a support person can find them.

Use the full printable handbook in its chapter order and write questions in the passport. You do not need to scan the QR or follow an internet link to use the essential treatment and safety information.
The NCCP regimen combines evidence and specialist guidance for a defined treatment setting.

A treatment name such as TPF or chemoradiation does not make different dose schedules, patient groups or sequences interchangeable. Ask which research and clinical factors support your exact plan. No single study percentage is presented as your personal chance of benefit.

required_units.text: Space for your own cycle or review record, questions and notes, followed by your treatment card.
TCF induction followed by carboplatin and radiotherapyNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00323

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.

Record the actual date, treatment phase, medicines given, any delay or dose change, blood tests and next appointments. The treating service confirms all entries; this does not replace its clinical record.

rows.label: Docetaxel
rows.text: Docetaxel 75 mg/m² by IV infusion over 60 minutes on Day 1.

rows.label: Cisplatin and fluids
rows.text: Cisplatin 100 mg/m² over 2 hours, with prescribed hydration.

rows.label: Fluorouracil infusions
rows.text: Fluorouracil 1,000 mg/m² per day runs continuously over 96 hours on Days 1–4; the source also allows a separate 22-hour infusion on each of those four days.

rows.label: Symptoms and recovery

Tell your team about new symptoms.1Hair and scalpDocetaxelHair thinning or loss can occur. Ask about scalp care and practical support.3Mouth and throatDocetaxel + 5-FUSoreness or ulcers (mucositis) can make eating and drinking difficult. Contact the team for pain or poor intake.5Blood and infectionDocetaxel + cisplatin + 5-FULow white cells can cause serious infection; low platelets cause bruising or bleeding; anaemia causes fatigue. Call for fever or sudden illness.7Stomach and bowelAll three chemotherapy drugsNausea and vomiting can occur; 5-FU may cause severe diarrhoea. Persistent symptoms can cause dehydration and need prompt help.9Hands, feet and nervesDocetaxel + cisplatinNumbness or tingling (peripheral neuropathy) can persist. Report difficulty with buttons, walking or balance before another dose.123456789102Ears and hearingCisplatinRinging or hearing loss can persist (ototoxicity). Report a change before the next dose.4Heart and chest5-FUChest pain can signal a heart effect (cardiotoxicity). Seek urgent assessment during or after the infusion.6Kidneys and fluidsCisplatinKidney injury and mineral changes can occur. Prescribed fluids and blood tests help protect you; report reduced urine or inability to drink.8Skin, nails, hands and feetDocetaxel + 5-FUDocetaxel may affect nails and retain fluid; 5-FU may cause painful palms or soles (hand–foot syndrome). Report swelling, pain or skin breakdown.10Later radiation areaRadiotherapy: later phaseDry mouth, taste change, sore skin and swallowing difficulty can build up. Some dental, saliva and swallowing effects last; follow the radiation care plan.Selected effects, not every possible effect or a prediction. Blood-count, skin and line markers are schematic. unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, sudden confusion, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms needs urgent assessment even if dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (a medicine-processing enzyme) (DPD) testing was normal. Report reduced urine, hearing change, ringing in the ears or new numbness promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112 or 999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.

This chemotherapy is given before definitive treatment to shrink or control the head and neck cancer. The team explains how induction fits your overall treatment aim and why this particular schedule is appropriate.

Docetaxel stabilises tiny structures called microtubules. Cells need these to separate their chromosomes during division; disrupting the process can stop cancer cells multiplying. Healthy dividing cells are also affected.
What to watch forTake prescribed steroid premedication. Report fever, lasting numbness, swelling, sore nails or infusion symptoms.

Cisplatin links strands of DNA, the instructions inside cells, making it harder for cancer cells to repair damage and divide. Healthy cells may also be affected. Kidney function, hearing, blood counts and nerve symptoms help the team decide whether the next dose is safe.
What to watch forReport reduced urine, persistent vomiting, tinnitus, hearing change or new tingling.

Fluorouracil, often shortened to 5-FU, interferes with the building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, which cells need to grow. It runs through a vein over the prescribed hours. Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) is an enzyme that breaks it down. Testing for DPD deficiency before treatment reduces risk but cannot rule out every severe reaction.
What to watch forReport severe diarrhoea, mouth sores, chest pain, sudden confusion, sore palms or soles, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms.

Carboplatin interferes with DNA repair and cell division. Its dose is calculated from kidney function. Blood counts can fall, including platelets that help stop bleeding. It is a different prescription from cisplatin. In this pathway it is used later, during radiotherapy, rather than alongside induction cisplatin.
What to watch forReport fever, unusual bruising or bleeding, marked tiredness or an infusion reaction.

Radiotherapy directs radiation at a carefully planned area. It is delivered on its own appointment calendar. Effects depend on which tissues receive radiation and can build up during the course or continue after it finishes.
What to watch forReport difficulty swallowing, weight loss, mouth pain, skin breakdown or problems managing saliva.

Docetaxel 75 mg/m² and cisplatin 100 mg/m² are given on Day 1. Fluorouracil 1,000 mg/m² per day runs continuously over 96 hours on Days 1–4; the source also allows a separate 22-hour infusion on each of those four days. Induction repeats every 21 days for 3 planned cycles unless cancer progression or unacceptable side effects require a change.

If the cancer has not progressed and blood counts have recovered adequately, the planned next phase is carboplatin AUC 1.5 once weekly with radiotherapy for seven weeks (NCCP 00332). The oncology and radiation teams must confirm the actual transition date: the source documents use different anchors for the 3–8 week interval. Surgery may be considered afterwards; it is not automatic.
Routine blood safety checks are different from tests ordered for a symptom and from scans used to assess the cancer. Your team supplies exact dates and explains results.
Blood and organ tests

Before starting: full blood count, kidney and liver tests, and DPD assessment before first fluorouracil unless already tested. electrocardiogram (ECG) is needed for compromised heart function; hearing assessment and measured kidney clearance are arranged when indicated. Discuss hearing, tinnitus, nerve symptoms, swallowing, weight, medicines and allergies.

Full blood count and kidney and liver tests are required before each cycle. Report hearing, tinnitus, nerve, mouth, bowel and fluid-intake changes before dosing; additional tests depend on symptoms and results.
Report symptoms promptly; extra blood or organ tests may be needed.
The team reviews recovery, results and earlier side effects before another dose or phase.

The team follows recovery and response before the next stage, including persistent kidney, hearing, nerve, mouth or bowel effects. Dental, nutrition and swallowing support may continue. Scans, examinations and any radiation-related late-effect tests follow your individual plan; no universal scan or blood tumour-marker schedule is set here.

If there is no progressive disease and marrow function is adequate, the source describes weekly carboplatin AUC 1.5 with radiotherapy for 7 weeks, followed by consideration of surgery. NCCP 00323 says start 3–8 weeks (Days 22–56) after the START of induction cycle 3. Its carboplatin cross-reference says 00322, whereas the matching current regimen is 00332. The 00332 indication text says after COMPLETION of induction, while its treatment paragraph says after START of cycle 3. Docetaxel premedication is dexamethasone 8 mg orally twice daily for 3 days starting the day before docetaxel; at least 3 doses should precede treatment unless contraindicated. If oral premedication was missed, the source permits dexamethasone 20 mg IV at consultant discretion. This is not automatic permission to proceed. Reconcile the total steroid with antiemetic dexamethasone; do not add both schedules blindly.

Prescribe cisplatin pre- and post-hydration and electrolytes using current renal/cardiac status and local policy. The national source suggests saline/magnesium with optional potassium, but a reference list is not an individual fluid prescription. Monitor intake, urine output, renal function and electrolytes.

granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (white-cell growth support) (G-CSF) may be used. There are no guaranteed “safe days”. Use your treating service’s written temperature threshold and urgent-contact plan. Fever, shivering or sudden illness can be serious even without a high temperature. Do not wait for the next visit. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure needs emergency help: call 112 or 999.

Docetaxel and cisplatin are given in the unit with prescribed premedication, fluids and anti-sickness medicines. Fluorouracil begins. Confirm whether your prescription uses one continuous 96-hour fluorouracil infusion or four daily 22-hour infusions; the unit writes down connection, change and disconnection times. Tell the team if steroid doses were missed, you feel unwell or you have new symptoms before treatment starts.

Fluorouracil 1,000 mg/m² per day runs continuously over 96 hours on Days 1–4; the source also allows a separate 22-hour infusion on each of those four days. Only trained staff connect, program, change or disconnect the infusion. Follow the line and pump instructions. Call for leakage, pain, swelling, damage or an infusion that appears to finish unexpectedly or stop.

Follow the prescribed home medicine and growth-factor plan. Side effects may continue or appear between visits; no day is guaranteed free of risk. Keep blood-test and review appointments and call promptly if unwell.
From preparing the line to coming home after disconnection. Your team arranges the appointments and shows you what to do.
Your team chooses the venous access device and teaches its care, including a port or peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) if used.
Confirm whether your prescription uses one continuous 96-hour fluorouracil infusion or four daily 22-hour infusions; the unit writes down connection, change and disconnection times.
Only trained staff connect, program or change the infusion. Do not calculate or alter the rate.
Call for leakage, pain, swelling, damage, disconnection, unexpected completion or a pump that appears not to run. Follow the unit’s device-specific emergency instructions.
The actual connection time and selected infusion duration determine completion. Do not disconnect or reconnect the line yourself.
Keep dressing, flushing and review appointments; report redness, pain, fever or swelling.

A port is a small chamber beneath the skin, usually on the chest, attached to a tube ending in a large vein. A special needle goes through the skin into the port when it is used. A PICC enters a vein in the upper arm; a short section remains outside under a dressing. Both can deliver a home infusion. Your team helps choose the device and teaches its care.

Tell the team about allergies, blood thinners, infections and any other cancer medicines. Follow the instructions about eating, drinking and transport; do not stop medicines yourself. Port placement uses local anaesthetic, sometimes with sedation or general anaesthetic. The team explains the procedure and risks, including infection, bleeding, clots and insertion complications. Ask how to manage discomfort, protect the wound and resume activity. Report increasing pain, redness, swelling, discharge or fever.

The nurse checks the line and treatment, secures the connection and dressing, and starts the pump. Before leaving, you should have the disconnection location and time, contact numbers including out of hours, and the written spill instructions. Ask to be shown what normal pump progress looks like. You do not need to calculate a rate.

Use the supplied carrier and the position recommended for your pump. Keep tubing free from pulling and kinks. Ask how to place the pump safely for sleep and how to protect the line and dressing when washing. Do not immerse it or swim. Avoid direct heat and cold. An elastomeric pump has a balloon that shrinks slowly and may have no alarm; an electronic pump has different instructions. Follow the instructions for the device you actually receive.

Keep the appointment even if the pump looks empty, unless the team changes the plan. Staff check the pump and line and arrange safe disposal. After flushing and other line care as required, the port needle may be removed and a small dressing applied. The implanted port stays in place until a separate removal procedure is arranged. A PICC remains in place and needs scheduled dressing and flushing care.

Call the team immediately if the pump leaks, is damaged, finishes unexpectedly early, appears not to run, or the line disconnects. Follow the emergency or spill steps you have been specifically taught, including use of a clamp if instructed. Do not reconnect, change settings or disconnect the pump yourself. Keep other people away from leaked medicine. If medicine touches skin, rinse it off and wash with soap and water, then seek advice.

Contact oncology immediately for pain or swelling around the line, a wet/loose dressing, redness, fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell. A painful swollen arm or neck needs urgent advice. Severe chest pain, major breathing difficulty or collapse: call 112 / 999. Do not wait for pump disconnection or the next clinic visit.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.
Confirm the exact regimen, treatment aim, baseline tests, transport, support medicines and verified urgent contact numbers. Bring a full medicine list and any hearing, nerve or swallowing concerns.
Keep one calendar for blood tests, treatment and any radiation, dental, nutrition or swallowing appointments. If an appointment is cancelled, ask the relevant teams to agree the revised plan.
Tell the team about travel, cost, work, caring responsibilities, communication or reading needs. Ask whether a support person or interpreter can attend and how treatment changes will be explained.
Check the next blood-test and treatment dates, medicine instructions and whom to call if unwell. Have the service confirm the daytime, out-of-hours and backup contact routes.

The source premedication is dexamethasone 8 mg by mouth twice daily for three days, starting the day before docetaxel, with at least three doses taken before infusion. It helps reduce allergy and fluid retention. Follow your prescribed plan. If doses are missed or you cannot swallow them, contact the unit before attending; the clinician decides the alternative.

Cisplatin has a high risk of nausea and vomiting. The team provides preventive and rescue anti-sickness treatment. Have all steroid doses reconciled on one list so the docetaxel premedication and anti-sickness prescription do not lead to accidental duplication.

Growth-factor support (G-CSF) may be prescribed according to your risks, blood counts and any earlier infection or low-count complication. It is not a universal all-cycle requirement in this source. If prescribed, confirm the product, injection dates and missed-dose instructions; fever or sudden illness still needs urgent contact.

Cisplatin requires prescribed fluids before and after treatment. Oral hydration is encouraged for the following 24 hours, adapted to your heart, kidney and swallowing needs. Ask for a practical individual fluid plan and call for much less urine, persistent vomiting or inability to drink.

An antibiotic may be added by the treating team according to the regimen and your situation. It is not a medicine to start from an old supply. Confirm the name, start and stop dates and important interactions; infection symptoms still need urgent contact.

Use the mouth-care and pain plan. Report ulcers, infection, poor intake or weight loss early. Dietitian and speech and language support can tailor intake and swallowing advice; arrange dental assessment before planned head and neck radiation.

Discuss fertility, pregnancy, breastfeeding and the medicine-specific duration of contraception before treatment. Bring medicines, supplements and allergies and check before adding over-the-counter or herbal products.
Keep your diagnosis, treatment name and agreed goal with your records.
Ask where the cancer started, what the biopsy shows and how far it has spread. Site, stage, previous treatment and general health affect the available options.
Induction treatment for locally advanced stage III or IV non-metastatic squamous cell cancer of the head and neck, followed by chemoradiation when appropriate.

Your team explains any HPV/p16, Epstein–Barr virus or other tumour tests appropriate to your cancer site. Not every site needs the same tests. These are different from blood, kidney and other medicine safety checks.
Discuss the whole plan and each stage before consenting.

This chemotherapy is given before definitive treatment to shrink or control the head and neck cancer. The team explains how induction fits your overall treatment aim and why this particular schedule is appropriate. Ask how the expected benefit and burdens compare with suitable alternatives and with your priorities.

The clinician may delay, change or stop treatment because of symptoms, test results, response or your preferences. Record which component is affected and what must happen before restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription.
Plan the appointments and practical support around the exact prescription.

Docetaxel 75 mg/m² and cisplatin 100 mg/m² are given on Day 1. Fluorouracil 1,000 mg/m² per day runs continuously over 96 hours on Days 1–4; the source also allows a separate 22-hour infusion on each of those four days. Induction repeats every 21 days for 3 planned cycles unless cancer progression or unacceptable side effects require a change. This 21-day picture describes induction only. Steroid premedication starts the day before docetaxel. Infusion finish times depend on the chosen prescription and actual start time; later radiation or chemoradiation has a separate calendar.

Write the actual date, phase, medicines and any change. Record a delayed or omitted dose clearly; it is not automatically made up. The wallet card gives a brief record and the passport keeps the fuller history.
Use the written home plan and contact route.
Effects may begin during treatment or develop later, and some build up over repeated doses. Call for a new, severe or worsening symptom even when a calendar calls the day a recovery day.

Keep prevention medicines, rescue medicines and regular medicines together on one reconciled written list. Record what you take and whether it helps. Do not double a missed dose or reuse an old prescription unless your treating team instructs you.

Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, sudden confusion, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms needs urgent assessment even if DPD testing was normal. Report reduced urine, hearing change, ringing in the ears or new numbness promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112 or 999.
Dental preparation and gentle daily care reduce avoidable problems.

Arrange dental assessment before head and neck radiation. The dental and oncology teams decide what treatment is needed and how much healing time is required; do not schedule extractions independently.

Follow the prescribed brushing, fluoride, rinse and pain-relief advice. Report ulcers, infection, new bleeding, difficulty wearing dentures or worsening jaw opening. Avoid starting a new mouthwash without checking if the mouth is sore.

Dry mouth can increase dental problems and some radiation effects last. Keep regular dental care and tell any future dentist that you have had head and neck radiation before invasive treatment. Your radiation/dental team plans any procedure.
The aim is adequate intake and comfort during treatment.
Record weight and report food or drink becoming harder to manage. Pain, taste change, dry mouth or nausea can each need a different response; a dietitian can adapt the plan to you.

The team may suggest food fortification, supplements or tube feeding when intake or swallowing safety requires it. A tube is a support option, not a judgement about how well you have tried to eat. Training and follow-up are needed.
Ask for a realistic drinking plan that accounts for kidney/heart problems and any feeding tube. Persistent vomiting, dizziness, markedly reduced urine or inability to drink needs urgent contact.
A speech and language therapist can help protect function.
Report coughing or choking with food or drink, a wet-sounding voice after swallowing, food sticking or repeated chest infections. The team may need to assess aspiration risk and safe textures.
Do swallowing or jaw exercises only as taught for your situation. Treatment and recovery can change what is comfortable and safe. Ask for reassessment when symptoms change.
Tell the team about changes in speech, voice or hearing. Ask for written instructions, communication aids, an interpreter or help involving a support person.
Practical adjustments can make the plan easier to follow.
Balance rest with manageable activity according to your ability and team advice. Ask for help if weakness, falls, sleep difficulty or pain interferes with daily life.
Ask for support to stop smoking and discuss alcohol with the team. Mouth irritation, medicine interactions and head and neck recovery can change what is safe for you.

Tell the team about anxiety, appearance or intimacy concerns, finances, travel and caring responsibilities. Ask which local supports are available; resources can be added to your record when confirmed.
The last treatment and the end of recovery are different milestones.

Your team sets the examination and imaging plan for your cancer and symptoms. Record who arranges each test and who will explain the result. New or worsening symptoms should be reported rather than saved for the next routine scan.

Keep the regimen name, treatment dates, ongoing medicines and relevant alert information. Tell future clinicians and dentists about head and neck radiation if you receive it, and about any persistent kidney, hearing, nerve or swallowing problem.
Keep essential instructions available on paper.

The three-page companion gives the essentials. Use the passport for the agreed plan, visits, test results, symptoms and questions. The wallet QR opens this exact treatment’s further information; it contains no personal clinical record.

Have the treating service enter and verify daytime, out-of-hours and backup numbers before relying on this pack. Keep the written contact and temperature instructions where you and a support person can find them.

Use the full printable handbook in its chapter order and write questions in the passport. You do not need to scan the QR or follow an internet link to use the essential treatment and safety information.
The NCCP regimen combines evidence and specialist guidance for a defined treatment setting.

A treatment name such as TPF or chemoradiation does not make different dose schedules, patient groups or sequences interchangeable. Ask which research and clinical factors support your exact plan. No single study percentage is presented as your personal chance of benefit.

Call the treatment unit before docetaxel. The clinician decides whether an alternative premedication or a change to the appointment is needed.
No. Testing reduces risk but cannot exclude every severe reaction. Unexpectedly early severe diarrhoea, mouth pain, illness, chest pain or confusion still requires urgent assessment.

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.

Record the actual date, treatment phase, medicines given, any delay or dose change, blood tests and next appointments. The treating service confirms all entries; this does not replace its clinical record.

TCF induction followed by radiotherapyNational Cancer Control Programme (NCCP) 00324

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.

Record the actual date, treatment phase, medicines given, any delay or dose change, blood tests and next appointments. The treating service confirms all entries; this does not replace its clinical record.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, sudden confusion, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms needs urgent assessment even if dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (a medicine-processing enzyme) (DPD) testing was normal. Report reduced urine, hearing change, ringing in the ears or new numbness promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112 or 999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.

This chemotherapy is given before definitive treatment to shrink or control the head and neck cancer. The team explains how induction fits your overall treatment aim and why this particular schedule is appropriate.

Docetaxel stabilises tiny structures called microtubules. Cells need these to separate their chromosomes during division; disrupting the process can stop cancer cells multiplying. Healthy dividing cells are also affected.
What to watch forTake prescribed steroid premedication. Report fever, lasting numbness, swelling, sore nails or infusion symptoms.

Cisplatin links strands of DNA, the instructions inside cells, making it harder for cancer cells to repair damage and divide. Healthy cells may also be affected. Kidney function, hearing, blood counts and nerve symptoms help the team decide whether the next dose is safe.
What to watch forReport reduced urine, persistent vomiting, tinnitus, hearing change or new tingling.

Fluorouracil, often shortened to 5-FU, interferes with the building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, which cells need to grow. It runs through a vein over the prescribed hours. Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) is an enzyme that breaks it down. Testing for DPD deficiency before treatment reduces risk but cannot rule out every severe reaction.
What to watch forReport severe diarrhoea, mouth sores, chest pain, sudden confusion, sore palms or soles, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms.

Radiotherapy directs radiation at a carefully planned area. It is delivered on its own appointment calendar. Effects depend on which tissues receive radiation and can build up during the course or continue after it finishes.
What to watch forReport difficulty swallowing, weight loss, mouth pain, skin breakdown or problems managing saliva.

Docetaxel 75 mg/m² and cisplatin 75 mg/m² are given on Day 1. Fluorouracil 750 mg/m² runs over 22 hours on each of Days 1–5. Induction repeats every 21 days for 4 planned cycles unless cancer progression or unacceptable side effects require a change.

If the cancer has not progressed and blood counts have recovered adequately, radiotherapy is planned 4–7 weeks after completion of chemotherapy. The radiation team confirms the actual dates and prescription. This is a later phase, not radiation given alongside all four TCF cycles. Surgery may be considered afterwards.
Routine blood safety checks are different from tests ordered for a symptom and from scans used to assess the cancer. Your team supplies exact dates and explains results.
Blood and organ tests

Before starting: full blood count, kidney and liver tests, and DPD assessment before first fluorouracil unless already tested. electrocardiogram (ECG) is needed for compromised heart function; hearing assessment and measured kidney clearance are arranged when indicated. Discuss hearing, tinnitus, nerve symptoms, swallowing, weight, medicines and allergies.

Full blood count and kidney and liver tests are required before each cycle. Report hearing, tinnitus, nerve, mouth, bowel and fluid-intake changes before dosing; additional tests depend on symptoms and results.
Report symptoms promptly; extra blood or organ tests may be needed.
The team reviews recovery, results and earlier side effects before another dose or phase.

The team follows recovery and response before the next stage, including persistent kidney, hearing, nerve, mouth or bowel effects. Dental, nutrition and swallowing support may continue. Scans, examinations and any radiation-related late-effect tests follow your individual plan; no universal scan or blood tumour-marker schedule is set here.

Docetaxel premedication is dexamethasone 8 mg orally twice daily for 3 days starting the day before docetaxel; at least 3 doses should precede treatment unless contraindicated. If oral premedication was missed, the source permits dexamethasone 20 mg IV at consultant discretion. This is not automatic permission to proceed. Reconcile the total steroid with antiemetic dexamethasone; do not add both schedules blindly.

Prescribe cisplatin pre- and post-hydration and electrolytes using current renal/cardiac status and local policy. The national source suggests saline/magnesium with optional potassium, but a reference list is not an individual fluid prescription. Monitor intake, urine output, renal function and electrolytes.

granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (white-cell growth support) (G-CSF) may be used. After complicated neutropenia, the source recommends prophylactic coverage in subsequent cycles (example Days 6–15). Select the product and schedule individually; this is not an all-cycle mandatory instruction.

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. Use your treating service’s written temperature threshold and urgent-contact plan. Fever, shivering or sudden illness can be serious even without a high temperature. Do not wait for the next visit. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure needs emergency help: call 112 or 999.

Docetaxel and cisplatin are given in the unit with prescribed premedication, fluids and anti-sickness medicines. Fluorouracil begins. Five 22-hour fluorouracil infusions on Days 1–5; confirm each change and the final disconnection time. Tell the team if steroid doses were missed, you feel unwell or you have new symptoms before treatment starts.

Fluorouracil 750 mg/m² runs over 22 hours on each of Days 1–5. Only trained staff connect, program, change or disconnect the infusion. Follow the line and pump instructions. Call for leakage, pain, swelling, damage or an infusion that appears to finish unexpectedly or stop.

Follow the prescribed home medicine and growth-factor plan. Side effects may continue or appear between visits; no day is guaranteed free of risk. Keep blood-test and review appointments and call promptly if unwell.
From preparing the line to coming home after disconnection. Your team arranges the appointments and shows you what to do.
Your team chooses the venous access device and teaches its care, including a port or peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) if used.
Five 22-hour fluorouracil infusions on Days 1–5; confirm each change and the final disconnection time.
Only trained staff connect, program or change the infusion. Do not calculate or alter the rate.
Call for leakage, pain, swelling, damage, disconnection, unexpected completion or a pump that appears not to run. Follow the unit’s device-specific emergency instructions.
The actual connection time and selected infusion duration determine completion. Do not disconnect or reconnect the line yourself.
Keep dressing, flushing and review appointments; report redness, pain, fever or swelling.

A port is a small chamber beneath the skin, usually on the chest, attached to a tube ending in a large vein. A special needle goes through the skin into the port when it is used. A PICC enters a vein in the upper arm; a short section remains outside under a dressing. Both can deliver a home infusion. Your team helps choose the device and teaches its care.

Tell the team about allergies, blood thinners, infections and any other cancer medicines. Follow the instructions about eating, drinking and transport; do not stop medicines yourself. Port placement uses local anaesthetic, sometimes with sedation or general anaesthetic. The team explains the procedure and risks, including infection, bleeding, clots and insertion complications. Ask how to manage discomfort, protect the wound and resume activity. Report increasing pain, redness, swelling, discharge or fever.

The nurse checks the line and treatment, secures the connection and dressing, and starts the pump. Before leaving, you should have the disconnection location and time, contact numbers including out of hours, and the written spill instructions. Ask to be shown what normal pump progress looks like. You do not need to calculate a rate.

Use the supplied carrier and the position recommended for your pump. Keep tubing free from pulling and kinks. Ask how to place the pump safely for sleep and how to protect the line and dressing when washing. Do not immerse it or swim. Avoid direct heat and cold. An elastomeric pump has a balloon that shrinks slowly and may have no alarm; an electronic pump has different instructions. Follow the instructions for the device you actually receive.

Keep the appointment even if the pump looks empty, unless the team changes the plan. Staff check the pump and line and arrange safe disposal. After flushing and other line care as required, the port needle may be removed and a small dressing applied. The implanted port stays in place until a separate removal procedure is arranged. A PICC remains in place and needs scheduled dressing and flushing care.

Call the team immediately if the pump leaks, is damaged, finishes unexpectedly early, appears not to run, or the line disconnects. Follow the emergency or spill steps you have been specifically taught, including use of a clamp if instructed. Do not reconnect, change settings or disconnect the pump yourself. Keep other people away from leaked medicine. If medicine touches skin, rinse it off and wash with soap and water, then seek advice.

Contact oncology immediately for pain or swelling around the line, a wet/loose dressing, redness, fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell. A painful swollen arm or neck needs urgent advice. Severe chest pain, major breathing difficulty or collapse: call 112 / 999. Do not wait for pump disconnection or the next clinic visit.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.
Confirm the exact regimen, treatment aim, baseline tests, transport, support medicines and verified urgent contact numbers. Bring a full medicine list and any hearing, nerve or swallowing concerns.
Keep one calendar for blood tests, treatment and any radiation, dental, nutrition or swallowing appointments. If an appointment is cancelled, ask the relevant teams to agree the revised plan.
Tell the team about travel, cost, work, caring responsibilities, communication or reading needs. Ask whether a support person or interpreter can attend and how treatment changes will be explained.
Check the next blood-test and treatment dates, medicine instructions and whom to call if unwell. Have the service confirm the daytime, out-of-hours and backup contact routes.

The source premedication is dexamethasone 8 mg by mouth twice daily for three days, starting the day before docetaxel, with at least three doses taken before infusion. It helps reduce allergy and fluid retention. Follow your prescribed plan. If doses are missed or you cannot swallow them, contact the unit before attending; the clinician decides the alternative.

Cisplatin has a high risk of nausea and vomiting. The team provides preventive and rescue anti-sickness treatment. Have all steroid doses reconciled on one list so the docetaxel premedication and anti-sickness prescription do not lead to accidental duplication.

Growth-factor support (G-CSF) may be prescribed according to your risks, blood counts and any earlier infection or low-count complication. It is not a universal all-cycle requirement in this source. If prescribed, confirm the product, injection dates and missed-dose instructions; fever or sudden illness still needs urgent contact.

Cisplatin requires prescribed fluids before and after treatment. Oral hydration is encouraged for the following 24 hours, adapted to your heart, kidney and swallowing needs. Ask for a practical individual fluid plan and call for much less urine, persistent vomiting or inability to drink.

An antibiotic may be added by the treating team according to the regimen and your situation. It is not a medicine to start from an old supply. Confirm the name, start and stop dates and important interactions; infection symptoms still need urgent contact.

Use the mouth-care and pain plan. Report ulcers, infection, poor intake or weight loss early. Dietitian and speech and language support can tailor intake and swallowing advice; arrange dental assessment before planned head and neck radiation.

Discuss fertility, pregnancy, breastfeeding and the medicine-specific duration of contraception before treatment. Bring medicines, supplements and allergies and check before adding over-the-counter or herbal products.
Keep your diagnosis, treatment name and agreed goal with your records.
Ask where the cancer started, what the biopsy shows and how far it has spread. Site, stage, previous treatment and general health affect the available options.
Induction chemotherapy followed by radiotherapy for stage III or IV non-metastatic squamous cell cancer of the head and neck, following multidisciplinary assessment.

Your team explains any HPV/p16, Epstein–Barr virus or other tumour tests appropriate to your cancer site. Not every site needs the same tests. These are different from blood, kidney and other medicine safety checks.
Discuss the whole plan and each stage before consenting.

This chemotherapy is given before definitive treatment to shrink or control the head and neck cancer. The team explains how induction fits your overall treatment aim and why this particular schedule is appropriate. Ask how the expected benefit and burdens compare with suitable alternatives and with your priorities.

The clinician may delay, change or stop treatment because of symptoms, test results, response or your preferences. Record which component is affected and what must happen before restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription.
Plan the appointments and practical support around the exact prescription.

Docetaxel 75 mg/m² and cisplatin 75 mg/m² are given on Day 1. Fluorouracil 750 mg/m² runs over 22 hours on each of Days 1–5. Induction repeats every 21 days for 4 planned cycles unless cancer progression or unacceptable side effects require a change. This 21-day picture describes induction only. Steroid premedication starts the day before docetaxel. Infusion finish times depend on the chosen prescription and actual start time; later radiation or chemoradiation has a separate calendar.

Write the actual date, phase, medicines and any change. Record a delayed or omitted dose clearly; it is not automatically made up. The wallet card gives a brief record and the passport keeps the fuller history.
Use the written home plan and contact route.
Effects may begin during treatment or develop later, and some build up over repeated doses. Call for a new, severe or worsening symptom even when a calendar calls the day a recovery day.

Keep prevention medicines, rescue medicines and regular medicines together on one reconciled written list. Record what you take and whether it helps. Do not double a missed dose or reuse an old prescription unless your treating team instructs you.

Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe diarrhoea, severe mouth pain or inability to drink. Chest pain during or after fluorouracil, sudden confusion, or unexpectedly early severe symptoms needs urgent assessment even if DPD testing was normal. Report reduced urine, hearing change, ringing in the ears or new numbness promptly. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112 or 999.
Dental preparation and gentle daily care reduce avoidable problems.

Arrange dental assessment before head and neck radiation. The dental and oncology teams decide what treatment is needed and how much healing time is required; do not schedule extractions independently.

Follow the prescribed brushing, fluoride, rinse and pain-relief advice. Report ulcers, infection, new bleeding, difficulty wearing dentures or worsening jaw opening. Avoid starting a new mouthwash without checking if the mouth is sore.

Dry mouth can increase dental problems and some radiation effects last. Keep regular dental care and tell any future dentist that you have had head and neck radiation before invasive treatment. Your radiation/dental team plans any procedure.
The aim is adequate intake and comfort during treatment.
Record weight and report food or drink becoming harder to manage. Pain, taste change, dry mouth or nausea can each need a different response; a dietitian can adapt the plan to you.

The team may suggest food fortification, supplements or tube feeding when intake or swallowing safety requires it. A tube is a support option, not a judgement about how well you have tried to eat. Training and follow-up are needed.
Ask for a realistic drinking plan that accounts for kidney/heart problems and any feeding tube. Persistent vomiting, dizziness, markedly reduced urine or inability to drink needs urgent contact.
A speech and language therapist can help protect function.
Report coughing or choking with food or drink, a wet-sounding voice after swallowing, food sticking or repeated chest infections. The team may need to assess aspiration risk and safe textures.
Do swallowing or jaw exercises only as taught for your situation. Treatment and recovery can change what is comfortable and safe. Ask for reassessment when symptoms change.
Tell the team about changes in speech, voice or hearing. Ask for written instructions, communication aids, an interpreter or help involving a support person.
Practical adjustments can make the plan easier to follow.
Balance rest with manageable activity according to your ability and team advice. Ask for help if weakness, falls, sleep difficulty or pain interferes with daily life.
Ask for support to stop smoking and discuss alcohol with the team. Mouth irritation, medicine interactions and head and neck recovery can change what is safe for you.

Tell the team about anxiety, appearance or intimacy concerns, finances, travel and caring responsibilities. Ask which local supports are available; resources can be added to your record when confirmed.
The last treatment and the end of recovery are different milestones.

Your team sets the examination and imaging plan for your cancer and symptoms. Record who arranges each test and who will explain the result. New or worsening symptoms should be reported rather than saved for the next routine scan.

Keep the regimen name, treatment dates, ongoing medicines and relevant alert information. Tell future clinicians and dentists about head and neck radiation if you receive it, and about any persistent kidney, hearing, nerve or swallowing problem.
Keep essential instructions available on paper.

The three-page companion gives the essentials. Use the passport for the agreed plan, visits, test results, symptoms and questions. The wallet QR opens this exact treatment’s further information; it contains no personal clinical record.

Have the treating service enter and verify daytime, out-of-hours and backup numbers before relying on this pack. Keep the written contact and temperature instructions where you and a support person can find them.

Use the full printable handbook in its chapter order and write questions in the passport. You do not need to scan the QR or follow an internet link to use the essential treatment and safety information.
The NCCP regimen combines evidence and specialist guidance for a defined treatment setting.

A treatment name such as TPF or chemoradiation does not make different dose schedules, patient groups or sequences interchangeable. Ask which research and clinical factors support your exact plan. No single study percentage is presented as your personal chance of benefit.

Record each cycle separately. Each medicine has its own symptom table. Mark the worst symptoms since your last review, when they occurred and what they stopped you doing. Overlapping symptoms can be recorded under more than one medicine; you do not have to identify the cause.

These are patient-language severity prompts, not a validated questionnaire or a formal Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grading tool. Your team assigns the clinical grade. Serious symptoms override the columns: call without waiting to decide a severity level.
Use a new record sheet for each cycle or review. Copy or print another sheet when needed; the number of sheets does not prescribe the length of treatment.

Record the actual date, treatment phase, medicines given, any delay or dose change, blood tests and next appointments. The treating service confirms all entries; this does not replace its clinical record.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bruising or bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe mouth or throat pain, inability to drink or much less urine. Report new hearing changes, numbness, worsening swallowing, choking or skin breakdown promptly. During an infusion, tell staff immediately about rash, flushing, chest tightness, breathing difficulty or faintness. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112 or 999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.

Carboplatin and radiotherapy are used together as part of the treatment plan for head and neck cancer. The team explains the treatment aim, expected benefit and why this medicine and schedule suit your situation.

Carboplatin interferes with DNA repair and cell division. Its dose is calculated from kidney function. Blood counts can fall, including platelets that help stop bleeding. It is a different prescription from cisplatin. AUC is a prescribing target for drug exposure, not the number of milligrams in your bag; your clinical team calculates the dose using kidney function.
What to watch forReport fever, unusual bruising or bleeding, marked tiredness or an infusion reaction.

Radiotherapy directs radiation at a carefully planned area. It is delivered on its own appointment calendar. Effects depend on which tissues receive radiation and can build up during the course or continue after it finishes.
What to watch forReport difficulty swallowing, weight loss, mouth pain, skin breakdown or problems managing saliva.
The drawings are simplified explanations of drug action, not anatomical pictures or a prediction of response.

Your team confirms the active stage and dates. The full treatment guide explains each step.
This shows treatment timing, not guaranteed symptom-free days. Your team confirms the active phase and dates.

This phase follows induction chemotherapy. The source uses different reference points for the 3–8 week transition interval, so the oncology and radiation teams must confirm the actual start date after reviewing response and recovery.

Carboplatin AUC 1.5 is given by IV infusion over 30 minutes once every 7 days for 7 planned weekly doses, only while radiotherapy is being given. It must be stopped if the radiation course is cut short. Radiation sessions follow their own calendar.

After the planned chemoradiation course, the team reviews recovery and response and decides whether surgery or other treatment is appropriate. Induction and this weekly phase have separate prescriptions; later treatment is not automatic.

Routine blood safety checks are different from tests ordered for a symptom and from scans used to assess the cancer. Your team supplies exact dates and explains results.
Blood and organ tests

Before starting: full blood count, kidney and liver tests, plus measured kidney filtration (preferred) or an appropriate estimate for carboplatin dosing. Review prior treatment, medicines, hearing and nerve symptoms. Arrange dental, nutrition and swallowing preparation for head and neck radiation.

Full blood count and kidney and liver tests are required before every weekly cycle. Kidney results guide the carboplatin dose. Review infection or bleeding symptoms, mouth and skin pain, weight, intake and swallowing throughout radiation.
Report symptoms promptly; extra blood or organ tests may be needed.
The team reviews recovery, results and earlier side effects before another dose or phase.

Mouth, throat and skin symptoms can continue after the last session. The team follows blood-count recovery, nutrition, swallowing and any kidney, hearing or nerve problems. Keep dental care and the agreed radiation late-effect follow-up. Scans, examinations and any thyroid or other tests follow the individual treatment plan; there is no universal scan or tumour-marker timetable here.
Treatment and appointments
Confirm the exact regimen, treatment aim, prescription and appointment calendar.

Carboplatin AUC 1.5 is infused through a vein over 30 minutes. The dose in milligrams is calculated by the treating team using kidney function. Allow extra time for assessment, preparation and prescribed anti-sickness treatment, as well as separate radiation appointments. This weekly carboplatin regimen does not automatically require the cisplatin hydration or docetaxel steroid schedule from an earlier phase.
Follow the written support plan and record symptoms and medicines taken.
Record the final treatment dates and the named follow-up team.
Mouth, nutrition and swallowing
Agree oral care and assess weight, intake and swallowing. Arrange dental review before planned head and neck radiation.
Review mouth pain, weight, drinking, swallowing and, during radiation, the treated skin.
Report poor intake, choking, weight loss or inability to drink.
Dietitian and speech and language plans adapt to symptoms and recovery.
Continue dental, nutrition and swallowing care as needed.

Discuss symptoms and the agreed treatment aim.

Response, recovery and your preferences inform the next treatment decision.
Use your individual scan and clinic plan; this regimen does not set one universal scan or blood tumour-marker schedule.

Carboplatin dosing depends on kidney function. Measured GFR is preferred where feasible, with an appropriate estimate used when needed.

Helps plan safe intake, mouth care and prevention of avoidable radiation-related complications.
Assesses the cancer and informs further treatment.
Concurrent carboplatin and radiotherapy after induction for stage III/IV non-metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, subject to response and recovery.
Carboplatin AUC 1.5 intravenous (IV) every 7 days for 7 cycles, only while radiotherapy is being delivered. Discontinue carboplatin if radiotherapy is truncated.

Give carboplatin during radiotherapy as part of the planned combined treatment after induction. Carboplatin is a radiation partner in this phase; it is not a continuation of the TPF medicines.
