Symptoms and support
Days 1–7Symptoms can build up during treatment and continue afterwards. Call promptly if unwell.
Symptoms can build up during treatment and continue afterwards. Call promptly if unwell.

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. Use your treating service’s written temperature threshold and urgent-contact plan. Fever, shivering or sudden illness can be serious even without a high temperature. Do not wait for the next visit. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure needs emergency help: call 112 or 999.

Blood-test results, symptoms and the radiation plan are reviewed before carboplatin. The infusion takes about 30 minutes, but the whole appointment also includes assessment, preparation and any prescribed support medicines. Tell staff about new symptoms or any radiation cancellation before the infusion.

Attend radiation on its own calendar, follow the mouth, skin, nutrition and swallowing plan, and record symptoms. The weekly chemotherapy cycle does not imply seven daily radiation appointments. Call if eating, drinking, swallowing or pain control becomes difficult, or if you are unwell. Keep the next blood-test appointment.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.
Confirm the exact regimen, treatment aim, baseline tests, transport, support medicines and verified urgent contact numbers. Bring a full medicine list and any hearing, nerve or swallowing concerns.
Keep one calendar for blood tests, treatment and any radiation, dental, nutrition or swallowing appointments. If an appointment is cancelled, ask the relevant teams to agree the revised plan.
Tell the team about travel, cost, work, caring responsibilities, communication or reading needs. Ask whether a support person or interpreter can attend and how treatment changes will be explained.
Check the next blood-test and treatment dates, medicine instructions and whom to call if unwell. Have the service confirm the daytime, out-of-hours and backup contact routes.

Have one written list of preventive, rescue and regular medicines. Do not automatically continue steroid premedication, growth factor, antibiotics or cisplatin fluids from an earlier regimen; each requires a current prescription.

The team prescribes anti-sickness medicines according to this carboplatin schedule and local policy. Ask which medicines prevent symptoms, which are rescue doses and when persistent vomiting requires a call.

Arrange dental preparation before head and neck radiation. Follow the prescribed brushing, fluoride, rinse and pain-relief plan. Report ulcers, infection, bleeding or difficulty opening the mouth. Tell future dentists about radiation before invasive treatment.

A dietitian can adapt food, supplements or feeding support to your needs. Ask for a practical fluid plan that accounts for swallowing and heart or kidney problems. Call early for weight loss, poor intake or inability to drink.

Follow advice from your speech and language therapist on safe swallowing, exercises and textures. Tell the team about choking, a wet voice after swallowing, food sticking, hearing difficulty or communication needs.
Use the radiation team’s skin and pain plan. Symptoms may increase during the course or persist after it ends; ask for review when care is no longer controlling them.
Discuss fertility, pregnancy, breastfeeding and the medicine-specific contraception period. Bring medicines, supplements and allergies and check before starting new products.
Keep your diagnosis, treatment name and agreed goal with your records.
Ask where the cancer started, what the biopsy shows and how far it has spread. Site, stage, previous treatment and general health affect the available options.
Chemoradiation after TPF induction for locally advanced stage III or IV squamous cell cancer of the head and neck.

Your team explains any HPV/p16, Epstein–Barr virus or other tumour tests appropriate to your cancer site. Not every site needs the same tests. These are different from blood, kidney and other medicine safety checks.
Discuss the whole plan and each stage before consenting.

Carboplatin and radiotherapy are used together as part of the treatment plan for head and neck cancer. The team explains the treatment aim, expected benefit and why this medicine and schedule suit your situation. Ask how the expected benefit and burdens compare with suitable alternatives and with your priorities.

The clinician may delay, change or stop treatment because of symptoms, test results, response or your preferences. Record which component is affected and what must happen before restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription.
Plan the appointments and practical support around the exact prescription.

Carboplatin AUC 1.5 is given by IV infusion over 30 minutes once every 7 days for 7 planned weekly doses, only while radiotherapy is being given. It must be stopped if the radiation course is cut short. Radiation sessions follow their own calendar. This is one reference week of the concurrent phase, not a complete radiation calendar. If a radiation appointment changes, contact both teams before the next carboplatin dose; do not assume chemotherapy can proceed without the radiation course.

Write the actual date, phase, medicines and any change. Record a delayed or omitted dose clearly; it is not automatically made up. The wallet card gives a brief record and the passport keeps the fuller history.
Use the written home plan and contact route.
Effects may begin during treatment or develop later, and some build up over repeated doses. Call for a new, severe or worsening symptom even when a calendar calls the day a recovery day.

Keep prevention medicines, rescue medicines and regular medicines together on one reconciled written list. Record what you take and whether it helps. Do not double a missed dose or reuse an old prescription unless your treating team instructs you.

Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bruising or bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe mouth or throat pain, inability to drink or much less urine. Report new hearing changes, numbness, worsening swallowing, choking or skin breakdown promptly. During an infusion, tell staff immediately about rash, flushing, chest tightness, breathing difficulty or faintness. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112 or 999.
Dental preparation and gentle daily care reduce avoidable problems.

Arrange dental assessment before head and neck radiation. The dental and oncology teams decide what treatment is needed and how much healing time is required; do not schedule extractions independently.

Follow the prescribed brushing, fluoride, rinse and pain-relief advice. Report ulcers, infection, new bleeding, difficulty wearing dentures or worsening jaw opening. Avoid starting a new mouthwash without checking if the mouth is sore.

Dry mouth can increase dental problems and some radiation effects last. Keep regular dental care and tell any future dentist that you have had head and neck radiation before invasive treatment. Your radiation/dental team plans any procedure.
The aim is adequate intake and comfort during treatment.
Record weight and report food or drink becoming harder to manage. Pain, taste change, dry mouth or nausea can each need a different response; a dietitian can adapt the plan to you.

The team may suggest food fortification, supplements or tube feeding when intake or swallowing safety requires it. A tube is a support option, not a judgement about how well you have tried to eat. Training and follow-up are needed.
Ask for a realistic drinking plan that accounts for kidney/heart problems and any feeding tube. Persistent vomiting, dizziness, markedly reduced urine or inability to drink needs urgent contact.
A speech and language therapist can help protect function.
Report coughing or choking with food or drink, a wet-sounding voice after swallowing, food sticking or repeated chest infections. The team may need to assess aspiration risk and safe textures.
Do swallowing or jaw exercises only as taught for your situation. Treatment and recovery can change what is comfortable and safe. Ask for reassessment when symptoms change.
Tell the team about changes in speech, voice or hearing. Ask for written instructions, communication aids, an interpreter or help involving a support person.
Practical adjustments can make the plan easier to follow.
Balance rest with manageable activity according to your ability and team advice. Ask for help if weakness, falls, sleep difficulty or pain interferes with daily life.
Ask for support to stop smoking and discuss alcohol with the team. Mouth irritation, medicine interactions and head and neck recovery can change what is safe for you.

Tell the team about anxiety, appearance or intimacy concerns, finances, travel and caring responsibilities. Ask which local supports are available; resources can be added to your record when confirmed.
The last treatment and the end of recovery are different milestones.

Your team sets the examination and imaging plan for your cancer and symptoms. Record who arranges each test and who will explain the result. New or worsening symptoms should be reported rather than saved for the next routine scan.

Keep the regimen name, treatment dates, ongoing medicines and relevant alert information. Tell future clinicians and dentists about head and neck radiation if you receive it, and about any persistent kidney, hearing, nerve or swallowing problem.
Keep essential instructions available on paper.

The three-page companion gives the essentials. Use the passport for the agreed plan, visits, test results, symptoms and questions. The wallet QR opens this exact treatment’s further information; it contains no personal clinical record.

Have the treating service enter and verify daytime, out-of-hours and backup numbers before relying on this pack. Keep the written contact and temperature instructions where you and a support person can find them.

Use the full printable handbook in its chapter order and write questions in the passport. You do not need to scan the QR or follow an internet link to use the essential treatment and safety information.
The NCCP regimen combines evidence and specialist guidance for a defined treatment setting.

A treatment name such as TPF or chemoradiation does not make different dose schedules, patient groups or sequences interchangeable. Ask which research and clinical factors support your exact plan. No single study percentage is presented as your personal chance of benefit.
This source plans 7 weekly AUC 1.5 doses during radiotherapy, with each dose subject to safety review. Radiation has its own number of sessions and appointment calendar.
It is a target drug exposure used by the clinical team to calculate your carboplatin dose from kidney function. It is not a fixed milligram dose and is not a calculation you need to perform.

Contact both teams before the next carboplatin dose. This regimen is only given with radiation, and carboplatin must be discontinued if the radiation course is cut short. The teams confirm the revised plan.
Only if your team includes them in the new prescription. Induction steroids, growth factors, antibiotics and cisplatin fluids do not automatically carry forward.

Recovery varies and effects can continue after radiation finishes. Keep pain, dental, nutrition and swallowing support and report worsening symptoms; the last session does not mean support should stop.

unique_source_inventory.text: Severe breathing difficulty, collapse, seizure or severe chest pain: call emergency services. Do not wait for an online answer.

Temperature 37.5°C or higher, 36°C or lower, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell — even with a normal temperature. Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bruising or bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe mouth or throat pain, inability to drink or much less urine. Report new hearing changes, numbness, worsening swallowing, choking or skin breakdown promptly. During an infusion, tell staff immediately about rash, flushing, chest tightness, breathing difficulty or faintness. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112 or 999.

Follow the urgent contact instructions from your treating hospital. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Outside clinic hours, use your instructed out-of-hours pathway or the emergency department.
This page does not diagnose symptoms or decide whether it is safe to stay at home. You do not need to know which medicine caused a symptom before calling.

Carboplatin and radiotherapy are used together as part of the treatment plan for head and neck cancer. The team explains the treatment aim, expected benefit and why this medicine and schedule suit your situation.

Carboplatin interferes with DNA repair and cell division. Its dose is calculated from kidney function. Blood counts can fall, including platelets that help stop bleeding. It is a different prescription from cisplatin. AUC is a prescribing target for drug exposure, not the number of milligrams in your bag; your clinical team calculates the dose using kidney function.
What to watch forReport fever, unusual bruising or bleeding, marked tiredness or an infusion reaction.

Radiotherapy directs radiation at a carefully planned area. It is delivered on its own appointment calendar. Effects depend on which tissues receive radiation and can build up during the course or continue after it finishes.
What to watch forReport difficulty swallowing, weight loss, mouth pain, skin breakdown or problems managing saliva.

Carboplatin AUC 2 is given by IV infusion over 30 minutes once every 7 days for 6 planned weekly doses, only while radiotherapy is being given. It must be stopped if the radiation course is cut short. Radiation sessions follow their own calendar.

After chemoradiation, the team reviews recovery, response and whether any further treatment is appropriate. NCCP 00419 refers to later carboplatin/fluorouracil under 00552, but 00552 is specific to nasopharyngeal cancer. It is not automatically applicable to every head and neck cancer; any further chemotherapy requires a separately confirmed indication, prescription and start date.

Routine blood safety checks are different from tests ordered for a symptom and from scans used to assess the cancer. Your team supplies exact dates and explains results.
Blood and organ tests

Before starting: full blood count, kidney and liver tests, plus measured kidney filtration (preferred) or an appropriate estimate for carboplatin dosing. Review prior treatment, medicines, hearing and nerve symptoms. Arrange dental, nutrition and swallowing preparation for head and neck radiation. Audiology and formal nerve assessment are arranged when clinically indicated.

Full blood count and kidney and liver tests are required before every weekly cycle. Kidney results guide the carboplatin dose. Review infection or bleeding symptoms, mouth and skin pain, weight, intake and swallowing throughout radiation.
Report symptoms promptly; extra blood or organ tests may be needed.
The team reviews recovery, results and earlier side effects before another dose or phase.

Mouth, throat and skin symptoms can continue after the last session. The team follows blood-count recovery, nutrition, swallowing and any kidney, hearing or nerve problems. Keep dental care and the agreed radiation late-effect follow-up. Scans, examinations and any thyroid or other tests follow the individual treatment plan; there is no universal scan or tumour-marker timetable here.

Confirm the exact regimen, treatment aim, prescription and appointment calendar.

Carboplatin AUC 2 is infused through a vein over 30 minutes. The dose in milligrams is calculated by the treating team using kidney function. Allow extra time for assessment, preparation and prescribed anti-sickness treatment, as well as separate radiation appointments. This weekly carboplatin regimen does not automatically require the cisplatin hydration or docetaxel steroid schedule from an earlier phase.
Follow the written support plan and record symptoms and medicines taken.
Record the final treatment dates and the named follow-up team.

Agree oral care and assess weight, intake and swallowing. Arrange dental review before planned head and neck radiation.
Review mouth pain, weight, drinking, swallowing and, during radiation, the treated skin.

Dietitian and speech and language plans adapt to symptoms and recovery.

Discuss symptoms and the agreed treatment aim.

Response, recovery and your preferences inform the next treatment decision.
Use your individual scan and clinic plan; this regimen does not set one universal scan or blood tumour-marker schedule.
Checks infection-fighting white cells, red cells and platelets; low counts may require a delay or another change.
Carboplatin dosing depends on kidney function. Measured GFR is preferred where feasible, with an appropriate estimate used when needed.
Supports safe treatment review and investigation of changes.
Identifies new problems and effects remaining from earlier platinum chemotherapy.
Helps plan safe intake, mouth care and prevention of avoidable radiation-related complications.
Assesses the cancer and informs further treatment.

NCCP 00419a: stage III/IV locally advanced head and neck squamous cell carcinoma when cisplatin is contraindicated or not tolerated. This authored content is restricted to the head_neck context; cervical content remains separate.

Carboplatin AUC 2 intravenous (IV) every 7 days for 6 cycles with radiotherapy. This is the current NCCP 00419 v6 head and neck schedule; do not substitute the AUC 1.5 seven-cycle post-induction pathway.

Use carboplatin with radiotherapy when the team judges cisplatin unsuitable or not tolerated. The intended benefit and uncertainty must be discussed in the context of the patient’s disease, fitness and radiotherapy plan.

Symptoms and support
Days 1–7Symptoms can build up during treatment and continue afterwards. Call promptly if unwell.
Symptoms can build up during treatment and continue afterwards. Call promptly if unwell.

There are no guaranteed “safe days”. Use your treating service’s written temperature threshold and urgent-contact plan. Fever, shivering or sudden illness can be serious even without a high temperature. Do not wait for the next visit. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure needs emergency help: call 112 or 999.

Blood-test results, symptoms and the radiation plan are reviewed before carboplatin. The infusion takes about 30 minutes, but the whole appointment also includes assessment, preparation and any prescribed support medicines. Tell staff about new symptoms or any radiation cancellation before the infusion.

Attend radiation on its own calendar, follow the mouth, skin, nutrition and swallowing plan, and record symptoms. The weekly chemotherapy cycle does not imply seven daily radiation appointments. Call if eating, drinking, swallowing or pain control becomes difficult, or if you are unwell. Keep the next blood-test appointment.
Agree the arrangements with your oncology team.
Confirm the exact regimen, treatment aim, baseline tests, transport, support medicines and verified urgent contact numbers. Bring a full medicine list and any hearing, nerve or swallowing concerns.
Keep one calendar for blood tests, treatment and any radiation, dental, nutrition or swallowing appointments. If an appointment is cancelled, ask the relevant teams to agree the revised plan.
Tell the team about travel, cost, work, caring responsibilities, communication or reading needs. Ask whether a support person or interpreter can attend and how treatment changes will be explained.
Check the next blood-test and treatment dates, medicine instructions and whom to call if unwell. Have the service confirm the daytime, out-of-hours and backup contact routes.

Have one written list of preventive, rescue and regular medicines. Do not automatically continue steroid premedication, growth factor, antibiotics or cisplatin fluids from an earlier regimen; each requires a current prescription.
The team prescribes anti-sickness medicines according to this carboplatin schedule and local policy. NCCP 00419 classifies nausea and vomiting risk as moderate.

Arrange dental preparation before head and neck radiation. Follow the prescribed brushing, fluoride, rinse and pain-relief plan. Report ulcers, infection, bleeding or difficulty opening the mouth. Tell future dentists about radiation before invasive treatment.

A dietitian can adapt food, supplements or feeding support to your needs. Ask for a practical fluid plan that accounts for swallowing and heart or kidney problems. Call early for weight loss, poor intake or inability to drink.

Follow advice from your speech and language therapist on safe swallowing, exercises and textures. Tell the team about choking, a wet voice after swallowing, food sticking, hearing difficulty or communication needs.
Use the radiation team’s skin and pain plan. Symptoms may increase during the course or persist after it ends; ask for review when care is no longer controlling them.
Discuss fertility, pregnancy, breastfeeding and the medicine-specific contraception period. Bring medicines, supplements and allergies and check before starting new products.
Keep your diagnosis, treatment name and agreed goal with your records.
Ask where the cancer started, what the biopsy shows and how far it has spread. Site, stage, previous treatment and general health affect the available options.
Concurrent chemoradiation for locally advanced stage III or IV squamous cell head and neck cancer when cisplatin is contraindicated or cannot be tolerated.

Your team explains any HPV/p16, Epstein–Barr virus or other tumour tests appropriate to your cancer site. Not every site needs the same tests. These are different from blood, kidney and other medicine safety checks.
Discuss the whole plan and each stage before consenting.

Carboplatin and radiotherapy are used together as part of the treatment plan for head and neck cancer. The team explains the treatment aim, expected benefit and why this medicine and schedule suit your situation. Ask how the expected benefit and burdens compare with suitable alternatives and with your priorities.

The clinician may delay, change or stop treatment because of symptoms, test results, response or your preferences. Record which component is affected and what must happen before restarting. Do not restart from an old prescription.
Plan the appointments and practical support around the exact prescription.

Carboplatin AUC 2 is given by IV infusion over 30 minutes once every 7 days for 6 planned weekly doses, only while radiotherapy is being given. It must be stopped if the radiation course is cut short. Radiation sessions follow their own calendar. This is one reference week of the concurrent phase, not a complete radiation calendar. If a radiation appointment changes, contact both teams before the next carboplatin dose; do not assume chemotherapy can proceed without the radiation course.

Write the actual date, phase, medicines and any change. Record a delayed or omitted dose clearly; it is not automatically made up. The wallet card gives a brief record and the passport keeps the fuller history.
Use the written home plan and contact route.
Effects may begin during treatment or develop later, and some build up over repeated doses. Call for a new, severe or worsening symptom even when a calendar calls the day a recovery day.

Keep prevention medicines, rescue medicines and regular medicines together on one reconciled written list. Record what you take and whether it helps. Do not double a missed dose or reuse an old prescription unless your treating team instructs you.

Call oncology immediately for fever, shivering, sudden illness, unusual bruising or bleeding, persistent vomiting, severe mouth or throat pain, inability to drink or much less urine. Report new hearing changes, numbness, worsening swallowing, choking or skin breakdown promptly. During an infusion, tell staff immediately about rash, flushing, chest tightness, breathing difficulty or faintness. Severe chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, collapse or a seizure is an emergency: call 112 or 999.
Dental preparation and gentle daily care reduce avoidable problems.

Arrange dental assessment before head and neck radiation. The dental and oncology teams decide what treatment is needed and how much healing time is required; do not schedule extractions independently.

Follow the prescribed brushing, fluoride, rinse and pain-relief advice. Report ulcers, infection, new bleeding, difficulty wearing dentures or worsening jaw opening. Avoid starting a new mouthwash without checking if the mouth is sore.

Dry mouth can increase dental problems and some radiation effects last. Keep regular dental care and tell any future dentist that you have had head and neck radiation before invasive treatment. Your radiation/dental team plans any procedure.
The aim is adequate intake and comfort during treatment.
Record weight and report food or drink becoming harder to manage. Pain, taste change, dry mouth or nausea can each need a different response; a dietitian can adapt the plan to you.

The team may suggest food fortification, supplements or tube feeding when intake or swallowing safety requires it. A tube is a support option, not a judgement about how well you have tried to eat. Training and follow-up are needed.
Ask for a realistic drinking plan that accounts for kidney/heart problems and any feeding tube. Persistent vomiting, dizziness, markedly reduced urine or inability to drink needs urgent contact.
A speech and language therapist can help protect function.
Report coughing or choking with food or drink, a wet-sounding voice after swallowing, food sticking or repeated chest infections. The team may need to assess aspiration risk and safe textures.
Do swallowing or jaw exercises only as taught for your situation. Treatment and recovery can change what is comfortable and safe. Ask for reassessment when symptoms change.
Tell the team about changes in speech, voice or hearing. Ask for written instructions, communication aids, an interpreter or help involving a support person.
Practical adjustments can make the plan easier to follow.
Balance rest with manageable activity according to your ability and team advice. Ask for help if weakness, falls, sleep difficulty or pain interferes with daily life.
Ask for support to stop smoking and discuss alcohol with the team. Mouth irritation, medicine interactions and head and neck recovery can change what is safe for you.

Tell the team about anxiety, appearance or intimacy concerns, finances, travel and caring responsibilities. Ask which local supports are available; resources can be added to your record when confirmed.
The last treatment and the end of recovery are different milestones.

Your team sets the examination and imaging plan for your cancer and symptoms. Record who arranges each test and who will explain the result. New or worsening symptoms should be reported rather than saved for the next routine scan.

Keep the regimen name, treatment dates, ongoing medicines and relevant alert information. Tell future clinicians and dentists about head and neck radiation if you receive it, and about any persistent kidney, hearing, nerve or swallowing problem.
Keep essential instructions available on paper.

The three-page companion gives the essentials. Use the passport for the agreed plan, visits, test results, symptoms and questions. The wallet QR opens this exact treatment’s further information; it contains no personal clinical record.

Have the treating service enter and verify daytime, out-of-hours and backup numbers before relying on this pack. Keep the written contact and temperature instructions where you and a support person can find them.

Use the full printable handbook in its chapter order and write questions in the passport. You do not need to scan the QR or follow an internet link to use the essential treatment and safety information.
The NCCP regimen combines evidence and specialist guidance for a defined treatment setting.

A treatment name such as TPF or chemoradiation does not make different dose schedules, patient groups or sequences interchangeable. Ask which research and clinical factors support your exact plan. No single study percentage is presented as your personal chance of benefit.
This source plans 6 weekly AUC 2 doses during radiotherapy, with each dose subject to safety review. Radiation has its own number of sessions and appointment calendar.
It is a target drug exposure used by the clinical team to calculate your carboplatin dose from kidney function. It is not a fixed milligram dose and is not a calculation you need to perform.

Contact both teams before the next carboplatin dose. This regimen is only given with radiation, and carboplatin must be discontinued if the radiation course is cut short. The teams confirm the revised plan.
Only if your team includes them in the new prescription. Induction steroids, growth factors, antibiotics and cisplatin fluids do not automatically carry forward.

Recovery varies and effects can continue after radiation finishes. Keep pain, dental, nutrition and swallowing support and report worsening symptoms; the last session does not mean support should stop.
